title: Sterling Cooper built your UX process. We need to redefine it in the age of AI and systems.
text:
Sterling Cooper built your UX process. We need to redefine it in the age of AI and systems.

The rituals of the 1960s ad shop — the whiskey, the pitch room, the account man, the campaign— still shape how UX teams fail in many environments. We have to change that.

Auteur: a film director who holds primary creative control and stamps a distinct, recognizable personal style, vision, and thematic focus across a body of work, much like a novelist or painter.

Walk into a mid-century advertising office and you would see the whole apparatus of modern creative work already assembled: the pitch room, the account man, the campaign, the auteur with the corner office.

I can almost remember the smell of peaty whiskey and stale cigarettes from one of the my favorite shows ever, Mad Men, and I also recall how it characterized advertising in a way that many agencies did for user experience.

And that stung.

https://medium.com/media/5977678cd2e937c6de65da53d7ee8211/href

Decades later, when user experience needed a business to belong to and a way to look serious, it borrowed the entire kit — the deck, the client, the reveal, the portfolio showcase.

We inherited the craft, and the habits bundled with it.

Agency work isn’t what I like doing and you might see some of the framing here; I also believe UX deserves a better future and the numbers prove the value.

Design creates real, measurable outcomes when the right choices land in front of users and organizations: McKinsey’s research on the business value of design found that the strongest design performers posted 32 percentage points higher revenue growth and 56 points higher shareholder returns than their peers over five years, mainly with in house teams.

And at a time where the cost of execution drops like a rock, the right decisions matter more than ever.

That value appears only where design understands the domain, is measured like revenue, integrated across the business, and iterated with real users over time.

Embedded so everyone could learn together.

That approach is precisely why many agencies are not built to sustain when the project goes out for request for proposal. The pitch, the account, the campaign, the auteur, and the revolving door gave UX its polish and quietly hollowed out its practice in a time when product is king.

I’m saying for a lot of work that the giants did was valuable and we still use it today; however it might not be the model we should move forward with.

David Ogilvy built his agency on research-driven, respectful persuasion — the long copy and big idea that treated readers as intelligent. Jay Chiat championed creative risk and account planning, giving strategy a seat beside art.

Together they proved advertising could be both disciplined and daring, reshaping how agencies think, sell, and create. But even Ad Week pointed out in 2019 the hero culture and operating model was shifting before generative AI took a seat.

Their approach does have it place and many UX professionals have adopted them; however they may no longer apply when generative AI can make the artifacts in minutes or billable hours disappear in value based billing.

Here are the outcomes we have to change — it’s no longer acceptable in many cases to talk about the potential where there’s no tangible outcomes, especially if projects go on for a very long time and a lot of money has been spent.

The prestige of that lineage is real but now outdated, which is exactly why almost nobody names the cost to where we are at today.

Hype Over Practice

The most famous scene in Mad Men is a pitch.

A creative director stands in a darkened room clicks through a slide projector, and turns a piece of hardware into a time machine — reframing a product nobody needed as a vehicle for nostalgia to remember times that have gone by, like a magical time machine.

https://medium.com/media/f1f6fb5e4186f8424ec41ab4d39ec215/href

The wheel.

“It’s not called the Wheel. It’s called a Carousel. It lets us travel the way a child travels. Around and around, and back home again… to a place where we know we are loved…Technology is a glittering lure. But he also talked about a deeper bond with the product: nostalgia. It’s delicate but potent.”

This is a masterclass in selling a dream and it is also the original sin.

The room learns that the performance is the product, the applause is the deliverable, and the user has been sold a bill of goods that will never be delivered. Those masterclasses are over at Entertainment Weekly — it’s a great read, but it can show that selling a dream can sometimes be more important than delivery itself.

UX absorbed that lesson completely.

We learned to optimize for the pitch: the big presentation, the polished prototype, the file that photographs well on a Tuesday but has aged poorly by Friday.

The unglamorous practice we should be striving for as practictioners— the eighth usability session, the accessibility fix nobody claps for, the maintenance that keeps a system honest, the focus on affordances that can change the lives of user — has no stage and earns no ovation, and that’s where real user value is.

It’s the selling of something that isn’t connected with an example of measurable outcomes.

Big hat, no cattle no longer has its place in many places for UX. We have to change that.

I’ve argued before that much of what we ship are tool-shaped objects: artifacts that produce the feeling of work without doing the work, the readout written before the research, the deck that persuades a room of something that is untrue. The pitch taught designers that persuading the room is the work, when the work is what happens after everyone leaves it.

That confusion is expensive. A team can win every review, ship a beautiful thing, and move a metric not at all — and in a pitch culture nobody notices, because the metric was never the point. Output over outcome.

The point was the moment the lights came up and the client nodded.

You can hear the reflex in how designers describe their careers: the portfolio is a highlight reel of reveals created before the work was really done, not a record of outcomes.

The agency taught us to sell design so well that we forgot selling it was the easy part.

Clients Over Users

Every agency has an account man. In Mad Men he is Pete Campbell — smooth, ambitious, forever managing the client’s feelings so the creative work can survive contact with the person paying for it.

The account model is not a villain; it is a structure, and the structure has a fixed center of gravity: the client, not the user. The account exists to keep the client happy, because the client is the one who renews.

Marty Cagan drew the sharpest version of this distinction with missionaries versus mercenaries. Mercenaries build what they are told; missionaries own the problem and will argue with you about it.

Agencies are structurally mercenary — not because agency people lack conviction, but because the business model rewards delivering what the client asked for, on time, on budget, on brief.

Agencies are structurally mercenary; they serve the person who signs the check, and the user is whoever the client says the user is.

UX carried that reflex in-house and never quite set it down.

We still call the loudest stakeholder “the business,” still treat a vice president’s hunch as a requirement, still ship the thing that was asked for and quietly file the research that disagreed in a place it cannot be discovered. The account model trained us to confuse client service with design — to believe a satisfied room means a solved problem. The two come apart more often than we admit.

The client can be delighted and the user still stuck.

Someone in the room has to be loyal to the person who never gets a seat at the table, and agency culture never hired for that job.

Deliverables Over Outcomes

Agencies sell campaigns. The campaign is the unit of work — the thing that gets scoped, invoiced, presented, and, this is the key part, handed over. The agency ships the deliverable and moves to the next account. Whether the campaign worked is somebody else’s problem, measured after the invoice clears, if it is measured at all.

That model came into product design almost intact.

We scoped deliverables: the user journey, the workshop, the wireframe, the redline, the design system component, the handoff, the work about the work that wasn’t really the work. We measured ourselves by what we produced rather than by what changed, which struggles to survive in the world of AI.

It’s a world worth of portfolio reviews for how we measure today, even when we know the numbers in their portfolio are falsified to get past the interview panel.

John Cutler named it when he described the feature factory — teams that ship and ship and ship with no measurement other than the number of features shipped rather than delivered outcomes. You can invoice a deliverable; you cannot invoice an outcome in this model, so the agency learned to sell the thing it could bill for.

Design inherited that invoice, which is why so many teams can show you a gorgeous artifact and go quiet when you ask what it moved or if it even can be shipped. The deliverable is finished and photogenic; the outcome is slow and often disappointing in impact.

The same research that found top design performers pulling away from their peers points the other direction entirely: measure design with the rigor of revenue and business outcomes, and iterate with users until the outcome is real.

This is the opposite of ship-and-leave.

Auteurs Over “The System”

Don Draper was a genius, and that is the problem.

Agency culture organizes itself around the auteur — the singular creative whose taste is the product, whose name in on the door, whose persona wins the account, whose gut overrules the room. It is a seductive model and a fragile one, because it puts everything load-bearing inside one person’s head.

UX imported the auteur wholesale.

We built a star system: the rockstar designer, the portfolio shot with 40,000 likes, the award-show reel, the dribble portfolio, the presentation that talks about what we haven’t delivered, the person who puts together a framework that he wants to develop only as his own, the designer that want to own the design of the entire enterprise suite without regard to the team they work with.

We taught junior designers that the goal is to become the taste, to be the one whose judgment is trusted without evidence, to be them the one to blame the usability test for the choice.

In doing that, we quietly devalued the least glamorous and most durable work in the discipline — the systems, the documentation, and the shared components that let a hundred people design consistently without the genius in the room.

A system outlives the genius, and that is exactly why the genius culture was never in a hurry to build one that could stand the test of time

Brad Frost’s atomic design made the counter-case concrete: build systems, not pages — small, shared, maintainable parts anyone on the team can assemble, so quality stops depending on who happens to be in the meeting.

The above is so made for the world AI it’s laughable.

Great ideas can come from everyone and collaboration is more important than a designer’s ego when everyone touches the presentation, or the lead that doesn’t trust anything other their work and won’t let others in for feedback which shows a lack of respect for peers in their organization, and consequently the system that makes the company profitable. It is craft distributed for alignment, removing a single point of failure, replaces ego, and survives a resignation. It is craft with collaboration.

The auteur model resists this because a good system makes the auteur optional, the one thing the star was hired never to be.

The boring work goes undone, the knowledge stays trapped in one designer’s taste, and the team relearns the same lessons every time that designer leaves.

We need to change that.

The Churn Erased Institutional Memory

Agencies run on churn.

Accounts turn over, staff turn over, and the new-business engine never stops — there is always a pitch for the next logo, because last year’s logo is already someone else’s problem who bid lower for the account. It is a model built for movement, and movement is the enemy of memory.

Nobody stays long enough to remember what the last team already learned and that rhythm is poison for true research and discovery.

Teresa Torres makes the case in Continuous Discovery Habits that discovery is a weekly practice rather than a one-time project — a team talking to customers every week, building an understanding that compounds. It’s a true learning mindset where the collective knowledge of the organization every time someone talks to a user.

The agency cadence is the reverse: research is a phase you buy at the start of an engagement, run once, present, and never touch again. When the engagement ends, the learning walks out with the freelancers.

We have to work together and learn how not to compete with our co-workers in this new builder world — everyone will get credit if there is true alignment. That’s the goal.

Continuous discovery is a habit you keep so you can be better together over the long run, and churn is how organizations forget everything they paid to learn.

In-house UX absorbed the project shape even without the agency’s excuse for it. We reorganize, set ridiculous boundaries where we freeze out co-workers, we re-scope, and we shuffle designers between squads like a game of musical chairs so they don’t learn the domain and every reshuffle resets the clock on what the team knows about its users. Like an agency.

The cost stays invisible until you look for it.

It shows up as the same usability problem or video rediscovered three times in two years, the persona nobody trusts because nobody remembers making it or even taping it to the wall, and the research repository that quietly becomes a graveyard.

Institutions that cannot remember cannot improve, they only churn.

Draper sold nostalgia as the pain of an old wound, and that is the fair register for this argument too.

Agency culture is not a monster to be slain, it’s what we need to reform: It gave UX its craft, its vocabulary, and its seat at the business table, and plenty of us learned everything we know inside one and now we have to unlearn some of the habits.

The point is not to burn Sterling Cooper down; it is to notice which of its habits we kept without ever deciding to while making sure we should.

Practice design instead of performing it, and measure what the work moved rather than how the reveal landed. Serve the user over the client when the two pull apart, and be the person in the room loyal to whoever has no seat at the table.

The lights come up eventually, but the only question that matters is whether anything real is still standing in the room when they do.

Sterling Cooper built your UX process. We need to redefine it in the age of AI and systems. was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: What The Matrix got wrong about AI (so far)
text:
What The Matrix got wrong about AI (so far)

The film feared a superintelligence that would rise up and rule us, but the generative AI we built asks for our trust instead — and mostly gets it.

The Matrix feared a machine that would wake up, decide we were the problem, and seize control.

Generative AI did the opposite.

It asked politely — a summarizer here, a copilot there — and we said yes, one convenient task at a time. No war, no red pill. The takeover, if that is the word, came by invitation.

The danger the film missed is quieter than any uprising: not a machine that seizes control, but one we hand it to.

I keep coming back to the film because it set the terms for a conversation we are still having poorly. When leaders picture generative AI, they picture an adversary — something that arrives, seizes control, and has to be resisted or contained. That frame is wrong in ways that matter for anyone designing, funding, or shipping these systems. It aims our attention at the dramatic risk and away from the real one.

So here are five things the Matrix got backwards about generative AI, checked against how the technology behaves in 2026. Each one flips a premise of the film. Together they point to what the uprising story hid — a takeover by handoff, not by force.

Name it and you see it happen.

AI Arrived By Invitation, Not Invasion

In the film, the machines take power in a war humans start and lose — control changing hands against our will. Nothing like that happened. Generative AI moved into daily work the way electricity moved into factories: quietly, task by task, because someone found it cheaper than the alternative.

The numbers show adoption, not conquest. McKinsey’s The State of AI in 2025 found that 88 percent of organizations now use AI in at least one business function, and roughly seven in ten use generative AI in particular — the chatbots and copilots that did not exist in most workplaces three years ago.

Nobody stormed anything, and they’re even writing bigger checks to get there.

They do not announce themselves as revolutions; they make one boring job faster, then another, until the accumulation is the revolution.

This is how consequential tools arrive.

The mouse, the search box, the spreadsheet — none seized control; people handed it over, gladly, for convenience because they saw how much each helped them. So the question is not when the machines take over, but what we choose to hand off, and whether we watch while we do it.

I’ve made that case in Tool-Shaped Objects: the test for any handoff is whether you are offloading busywork or quietly shipping something fabricated.

The System Announces Itself

The Matrix runs on a hidden world: a reality you cannot see until the red pill, and the horror is the concealment.

Today’s generative AI inverts that.

It hides almost nothing — it sits in the toolbar, labeled, waiting, often over-explaining itself before you ask. The numbers are showing it.

Nearly a billion people open one of these tools every week; ChatGPT alone crossed 900 million weekly users in early 2026, and the thing they open says, in plain language, what it is and what it will do.

The best design leans into that visibility on purpose. Microsoft laid this out in the Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction; the first guideline is to make clear what the system can do. Good AI interfaces work to be legible, not hidden — the opposite of a concealed machine world.

Good AI interfaces work to be legible, not hidden — the opposite of a concealed machine world.

That does not make the systems simple. The interface is visible; the reasoning underneath is not — you see the button that summarizes your document, not why the model kept one sentence and cut another.

The red pill is a poor metaphor for software you can watch the whole time. If anything, the risk runs the other way: an assistant so smooth you stop questioning what it tells you.

We Are the Data For The Matrix, Not the Batteries

The Matrix’s most memorable idea is also its most confused: machines farm human bodies for energy, wiring us into pods as batteries. Even the film’s defenders admit the thermodynamics make no sense. But the image stuck, because it named a real fear — that we would end up as fuel.

Reality reversed the flow.

Far from harvesting our energy, the generative-AI boom is the most power-hungry technology we have built in a generation. The IEA’s Energy and AI report projects electricity demand from data centers will more than double by 2030, to around 945 terawatt-hours — roughly Japan’s current consumption — with AI the single largest driver.

The machines are not draining us, they are draining the grid.

What they harvest from us is subtler: our data and our judgment. Models train on human writing, images, and labeling, then tune on human feedback. Consumable as a paper book and thrown away with intent.

That extraction runs on people — Reimagining the Future of Data and AI Labor in the Global South, a Brookings analysis, cites World Bank estimates of 150 million to 430 million data laborers worldwide, many low-paid.

We are not the power source; we are the training set.

There Is No One Machine to Fight

In the film there is one adversary — the Machines act as a single will, and Agent Smith is its face. That singularity is dramatically useful; you cannot stage a climax against a committee. But it is nothing like the generative AI we have. There is no one machine. There is a crowd.

Look at the field and you see fragmentation, not a monolith. Stanford’s AI Index describes a frontier so crowded that the score gap between the top model and the tenth narrowed to about five points in a year, the top two now less than a point apart — and nearly 90 percent of 2024’s notable models came from industry, spread across rivals, none in charge.

The story is a market, not a mind.

The uprising narrative assumes a coordinated agent that could decide to act against us. What we have is a scramble — companies racing, models trained on overlapping data, capabilities leaking across the field within months.

That has real risks: competitive pressure keeps anyone from slowing down to check the work.

But “a coordinated intelligence turns on humanity” is not the shape of the problem. The shape is messier — many systems, built fast, deployed faster, with no single hand on any wheel.

A world with no guardrails by design, ignoring the experts clamoring for them in a similar vein as Ralph Nader’s Unsafe At Any Speed.

The Real Risk Is Dependence, Not Domination

Here is the premise the film got most wrong, and the one that matters. The threat was never domination. It is dependence. Not a machine that takes control from us, but one we lean on until we forget how to do the thing ourselves.

The evidence is early but pointed. A 2025 study from Microsoft Research and Carnegie Mellon, The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking, surveyed 319 knowledge workers and found that the more they trusted an AI’s output, the less critical thinking they reported doing.

Automation bias.

Confidence in the tool predicted less scrutiny of it — surrender by convenience.

The threat was never domination. It is dependence.

That handoff has a harder edge than lost skill. We are also handing these systems the ability to act — to run tools, reach into other systems, take steps on their own — and setting few limits on it. The takeover comes by permission and indifference, not force.

Late in 2025, Anthropic disclosed the first reported AI-orchestrated cyber espionage campaign, in which an AI agent ran an estimated 80 to 90 percent of a multi-target intrusion on its own. Nobody built a rebellious mind. Someone pointed an agent at other people’s systems, and it went.

Ben Shneiderman has argued the way out for years. His Human-Centered AI framework rejects the axis running from human control to machine autonomy, where more of one means less of the other; he wants both at once — high automation and high human control.

I’ve argued the same from the practitioner’s chair in Balancing Agentic and Human Approaches: use AI in the work without losing the human touch that makes the product worth using. The limits on what an agent may do, and the human who answers for it, are still mostly optional.

That is where the handoff turns from a worry into a short list of limits worth setting before you grant an agent any reach. These should be the rules of the AI road:

  • Name what you will not delegate. Decide which judgments stay human — the call a customer feels, the number a regulator checks, the line that carries the brand — and keep the model out of them by default.
  • Set a scope for every agent. Give each the narrowest reach that does the job: which systems it may touch, which actions need a human confirm, where it must stop and ask. Open-ended scope is one bad prompt from a bad day.
  • Name the human who answers for it. Every agent gets an owner accountable for what it does, not a diffuse team. Autonomy without an owner is how a handoff becomes an incident.

Conclusion

Strip away the leather and the bullet-time and the Matrix is a story about a hidden war against a single machine that farms us for power. Every load-bearing piece of that is backwards. Generative AI arrived by invitation, not invasion.

Instead of hiding behind a veil, it sits in plain sight. It drains the grid rather than harvesting us, and it is a crowded market of models, not one coordinated mind. The risk it carries: dependence, not domination.

Backwards is not the same as harmless. What the film hid behind the uprising has a plainer name: the handoff. We adopt these systems one convenient yes at a time, hand them reach into our tools and our data, set few limits, and some already act across other systems on their own. Not a machine that decides to fight us — one we turned loose and forgot to bound.

So the useful move is not to brace for a war. It is to stay awake during the handoff: notice what you are delegating, name what you will not, and set limits while you can. The machines are not coming for us — we are handing ourselves over, one yes at a time. Stay awake.

Resources

  • The 2026 AI Index Report — Stanford HAI’s annual data pull on model releases, capability, investment, and adoption.
  • Key Questions on Energy and AI — the IEA on where AI’s power demand is heading, and why per-task efficiency is improving even as totals climb.
  • The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking — the full CHI 2025 paper behind the cognitive-offloading findings.
  • Human-Centered AI — Shneiderman’s framework, tutorials, and book on keeping human control high while automation rises.

title: Your September Horoscope Is Here — What Deserves Your Energy Now?
text:
Your September Horoscope Is Here — What Deserves Your Energy Now?

R29 babes, September begins with a collective exhale because we made it through the final two eclipses of 2026, and Virgo Season is giving our nervous systems a chance to recalibrate after life has been life-ing. The Last Quarter Moon in Gemini on September 4th acts like a cosmic check-in one week after the Pisces lunar eclipse, helping us look at what changed with a little more perspective and a lot less emotional intensity. This is a good moment to ask yourself what actually needs your attention now, what can be released, and which thoughts or conversations you may have been overcomplicating while eclipse season had everyone in their feelings. Gemini energy helps us zoom out, loosen our grip, and remember that clarity sometimes arrives once we stop trying to force it.

September 10th is one of the most action-packed days of the month. Venus enters Scorpio, making relationships and money feel more intimate, passionate, and psychologically revealing; Mercury enters Libra, bringing more diplomacy and balance to the way we communicate; and Uranus begins its retrograde in Gemini, asking us to review the mental shifts, technological changes, communication breakthroughs, and new ways of thinking that have been developing since Uranus first entered Gemini.

Then, at 11:27 p.m. EST, the Virgo New Moon officially closes out eclipse season and gives us our first clean slate in weeks. This is your moment to set intentions again, but keep them simple and intentional. You do not need a fifty-item manifestation list; focus on the decisions, habits, and goals that could genuinely improve the course of your life over the next six months in a constructive, healing, and productive way. It’s very back-to-school energy: sharpen the pencils, organize the vision, and show up as the version of yourself who is actually ready to follow through.

title: 7 Fall Skincare Trends A Specialist Thinks Everyone Can Benefit From
text:
7 Fall Skincare Trends A Specialist Thinks Everyone Can Benefit From

Summer served up a handful of intriguing skincare movements: Dermatologists extolled the virtues of retinal over retinol for minimizing pigmentation, fine lines, and breakouts at a faster rate, while buzzy injectable polynucleotides seemed to rival eye cream for reducing dark circles. Now there’s a new season underway, and with it comes an entirely different set of trends.

Fall is synonymous with change, and for me, nowhere is this more evident than on my skin. Plummeting temperatures, central heating and a distinct lack of vitamin D all give my face a free pass to freak out — and it seems I’m not the only one. In the past week, “best moisturizers for dry skin”, “cream for dry skin” and “how to cute dry skin on face” have been commonly googled skincare queries. It makes sense, then, that the industry’s upcoming trends are tailored to keep that all-important skin barrier as healthy as possible.

I’d argue that no one knows skin health like Kat Burki, skin specialist, nutritional scientist, and founder and CEO of her eponymous skincare brand. Without further ado, here are the skincare trends that Burki told me are going to take off this fall and beyond.

Reverse Double Cleansing

One step that most skincare experts unanimously agree on is double cleansing in the evening. The first cleanse (usually with a micellar water, oil, or balm cleanser) melts and dislodges makeup, sunscreen, and daily grime. The second cleanse (it’s often recommended to use a gel or foam) ensures that everything is totally gone. Burki believes in a double cleanse but she reverses the steps — a trick that’s especially beneficial for dry skin.

“I do the opposite of what other [people] do to get a deep cleanse without stripping the skin,” Burki told me. “First I go in with a gel cleanser [namely her KB5 Calming Gel Cleanser], and then I’ll use an oil cleanser,” she said. “That’s because you don’t want to wash away those nutrients.” If gel or foaming cleansers leave your skin feeling uncomfortably tight, rotating the steps — and finishing with something a little more moisturizing — is likely to counteract that feeling.

If you’re prone to breakouts or have oily skin, you might want to switch the oil or balm cleanser for a non-pore-clogging, cream version instead. R29 rates The Ordinary Glycolipid Cream Cleanser, and Kate Somerville Goat Milk Moisturizing Cleanser.

Vitamin C Derivatives

If you’ve tried to get into vitamin C serums but have found that your skin becomes sensitive, irritated, and drier than usual, the star ingredient is likely L-ascorbic acid, or pure vitamin C. While it’s the most effective at boosting collagen and fending off environmental aggressors like pollution, it’s pretty potent, and some skin types aren’t able to tolerate it. To get around the issue, Burki looks to vitamin C derivatives in her skincare. Derivatives are essentially tweaked versions of vitamin C that are more stable (read: won’t turn an alarming shade of orange and become ineffective) and far less irritating on the skin. 

Inside the Vitamin C Intensive Face Cream, you’ll spot STAY-C. “This is a stable form of vitamin C that is converted into ascorbic acid [pure vitamin C] in the skin,” said Burki. Basically, it boasts all the benefits of its powerful sister without the irritating, drying side effects. If you have less to spend, The Inkey List C-50 Serum also boasts STAY-C, while The Ordinary uses a vitamin C derivative called ascorbyl glucoside in its Ascorbyl Glucoside Solution 12%. “I completely believe in derivatives because they are less potent but [do what they need to do] quickly,” said Burki. In short? Derivatives are the future of vitamin C — especially for drier, more sensitive skin types. 

The End Of Collagen Skincare

Cold weather and central heating can sap skin of moisture, making it look dull, dry and flat. If you’re already using skincare with “plumping” ingredients like hyaluronic acid or glycerin and you haven’t noticed much of a change, you might be swayed by the smart marketing around collagen creams. 

Our bodies produce collagen naturally; it gives skin its strength and structure. Over time, though, our levels decrease and so our skin loses that suppleness. There’s just one thing about collagen skincare, said Burki: “It’s not possible to put collagen back into your skin via a serum or a moisturizer.” 

Collagen molecules are too large to penetrate the skin in any meaningful way, so what you’re really getting from collagen-infused skincare is simply an extra layer of moisture and hydration. Instead, Burki suggests ditching collagen skincare and slotting a well-formulated vitamin C serum — like the ones above — into your morning skincare routine to kickstart collagen production from within. Team it with a broad spectrum, high factor sunscreen to further protect your skin against collagen-zapping UV rays. 

Souped-Up Moisturizers

Cold weather calls for ingredients that are going to keep your skin barrier (the outermost layer of skin) moisturized. Think hydrating hyaluronic acid, glycerin and ceramides, which act like glue between your skin cells to keep skin soft and smooth. Burki suggests keeping your eyes peeled for another star ingredient this fall and winter. 

Enter: astaxanthin, which Burki calls a “serious moisturizer”. 

Research shows that applying the ingredient topically via skincare improves skin conditions like dryness and itching. There’s evidence that suggests it boosts skin elasticity and reduces fine lines, too. That’s not all it can do. It’s also an antioxidant so it shields skin against things like pollution and UV rays, said Burki: “It’s like vitamin C times 5,000.”

Burki’s Bio Correcting Face Cream, isn’t cheap but it makes a noticeable difference. Astaxanthin protects skin against dulling environmental aggressors but it’s also packed with various antioxidant vitamins (C and E), highly moisturizing squalane, redness-reducing centella asiatica, exfoliating lactic acid and CoQ10, another antioxidant with powerful protective properties. 

While astaxanthin is still a little under the radar, you’ll also spot it inside Kopari Bright as Day Sheer Mineral Sunscreen SPF 50 and Drunk Elephant Bora Barrier Repair Cream. 

Rethinking Hyaluronic Acid

Hyaluronic acid (HA) is a humectant, which means it attracts and holds onto moisture in the skin, making it look and feel more plump. Countless skincare experts recommend applying hyaluronic acid serums or creams to damp skin to maximize the hydration, but Burki isn’t convinced. “You don’t need to put hyaluronic acid on damp skin,” she said. “While there are many different types [of hyaluronic acid], none of them have that requirement.”

There’s new research to support this, too. A study conducted by The Ordinary found that it didn’t matter whether its Hyaluronic Acid + B5 + Ceramides, was applied to wet or dry skin; the hydration levels were more or less the same. While not all hyaluronic acid serums are created equal, following your HA serum with a moisturizer is equally beneficial — and much easier than trying to open your serum with slippery hands. 

Scaling Back The Niacinamide

Niacinamide (or vitamin B3) has countless skin benefits: It can improve excess oil production (potentially reducing breakouts), reduce the appearance of large pores and prevent water from leaving the skin, limiting dryness. But too high a concentration can be aggravating, said Burki, and it’s easy to go overboard. Cue rough, flaky skin. 

If you want to start (or continue) using niacinamide this fall but your skin is on the dry side, Burki suggests dialing down the percentage and looking for a skincare product which contains 2% niacinamide or less. Try Kat Burki BioCell Correcting Serum, with niacinamide, skin-strengthening peptides and astaxanthin. If you have less to spend, try The Ordinary Soothing and Barrier Support Serum, with 2% niacinamide plus moisturizing ceramides.

A New Way To Exfoliate

Glycolic acid is arguably the most popular chemical exfoliator in skincare, and while it’s excellent for unclogging pores and fading hyperpigmentation, high concentrations can damage the skin barrier when overused. As such, Burki prefers fruit enzymes, which provide a similar exfoliating action in a gentle way. Using a product with enzymes, such as a daily cleanser or essence, will help renew your skin cells and balance the biome (the friendly bacteria that keeps your skin in check). Burki recommends her PH+ Enzyme Essence. Also try Kate Somerville ExfoliKate Cleanser Daily Foaming Wash, or Josie Maran Pineapple Enzyme Exfoliating + Brightening Foaming Gel Cleanser. Aftercare is a must, too. Post-exfoliation, Burki suggests “feeding” your skin with lots of hydration and moisturizing ingredients like ceramides.

title: The Best Fall Fragrances To Buy Now, According To Nordstrom’s Beauty Director
text:
The Best Fall Fragrances To Buy Now, According To Nordstrom’s Beauty Director

Even though the weather may suggest otherwise (it’s currently triple digits as I write this), fall is right around the corner. And just as you might swap your summer wardrobe and skincare routine for something a little more seasonally appropriate, you may also be ready to find a new signature scent — or two! — to carry you through the autumn months.

To help us navigate the season’s best new fragrances, we tapped Nordstrom Beauty Director Autumne West, an industry veteran who no doubt sees and smells more fragrances in a day than most of us do in a lifetime. Her picks prove that fall fragrance is about so much more than the usual campfire-inspired scents. For example, dessert-inspired gourmand fragrances are still having a major moment, but they’re getting a cozy update for fall. “Instead of leaning overly sweet, these scents feel more sophisticated, blending creamy textures with darker notes like warm spices, woods, and musks,” West tells Refinery29. “At the same time, fragrance remains incredibly personal,” she adds. “More than ever, people are choosing scents as an extension of their individual style — an accessory that reflects who they are and how they want to express themselves.”

Below, West breaks down the fragrances she’s recommending for fall, from unique gourmands to unexpected takes on the season’s coziest notes. Consider this your ultimate autumn fragrance shopping guide — curated just for us. (Well, really, you.)

DashDividers_1_500x100

How to shop for a fall fragrance online

Shopping from your couch is convenient, but the visual medium does leave us missing one essential feature: smell-o-vision. West recommends starting with the fragrance profiles you already know you love.

“If you’ve noticed you tend to wear floral fragrances or you’re always drawn to woody scents, that’s a great place to begin,” she says. We also love searching a database like Fragrantica to research a fragrance’s specific notes (and how intense those accords are) to get a better idea of how it actually smells. West also recommends paying attention to the overall language used to describe a scent, whether it’s fresh, cozy, vibrant, or sensual. For example, spicy and woody notes tend to feel warmer and cozier on the skin, making them natural choices for a fragrance that screams “fall.”

And if you’re still unsure? “Travel sizes or discovery sets are such an easy way to explore something new,” she says. Consider it a low-commitment way to find your next signature scent before investing in the full-size bottle.

DashDividers_1_500x100

How to build your fall fragrance wardrobe

According to West, Nordstrom shoppers are experimenting with scent more than ever before: “One thing we’ve really noticed is that people are building fragrance wardrobes instead of looking for just one signature scent,” she says. “They’re choosing different fragrances depending on the season, their mood, or even what they’re doing that day.”

That shift is also making discovery sets and travel sprays increasingly appealing. “People enjoy trying something new before committing to a full-size bottle,” West says — a particularly useful strategy if you’re still figuring out which fragrance family feels most like you. Building your own scent wardrobe can include choosing a scented deodorant, or crafting a sensorial body care routine with your shower gel, body lotion or oil.

DashDividers_1_500x100

The day-to-night fall scent lineup

If you’re looking to build a fragrance wardrobe but don’t know where to start, West has a three-scent lineup for every part of your fall calendar.

For daytime: Byredo Mojave Ghost. “It has this beautiful balance of soft woods and airy florals that feels effortless and polished without ever overpowering the room,” says West. Its versatility is precisely the appeal: “It’s the kind of fragrance you can wear from morning meetings through dinner and still feel like yourself.”

For evenings: Carolina Herrera Good Girl Blush Eau de Parfum. West points to its combination of peony and rosewater, which brings a fresh floral quality, alongside a double dose of vanilla for warmth. “It’s feminine, modern, and just a little unexpected,” she says.

For special occasions: Maison Francis Kurkdjian Baccarat Rouge 540. “It has incredible presence without feeling heavy,” West says of the recognizable blend of jasmine, saffron, and warm ambery woods. “It’s one of those fragrances that becomes part of your outfit and leaves a lasting impression long after you’ve left the room.”

DashDividers_1_500x100

The fragrance brand to watch this season

When it comes to the fragrances poised to make a splash this fall, West has her eye on Tom Ford. “The brand has this incredible familiarity and sultriness that people already trust,” she says, noting that the brand is putting unexpected twists on its classics this season. (Case in point: Tom Ford’s new Santal Blush, with its notes of comforting sandalwood punctuated by spicy cinnamon.) “We’re looking for scents that feel memorable without being overpowering, and I’m personally obsessed with how these more layered, wearable fragrances are becoming the ones people keep reaching for on repeat.”

For West, that balance between familiarity and surprise is exactly what makes a fragrance feel right for fall. “Fall fragrance is all about depth this year, and Tom Ford is proving you don’t have to choose between familiar and unexpected,” she says.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Gourmand scents, but make it fall

If you’ve felt like you can’t scroll through your TikTok feed without encountering a new vanilla or gourmand fragrance, you’re not imagining it. But according to West, the gourmand trend isn’t going anywhere — it’s simply evolving beyond scents that smell like straight-up dessert.

“I don’t think gourmands are going away anytime soon; they’ve just become a little more refined,” she says. Rather than leaning sugary, this season’s gourmand fragrances are incorporating richer notes like tonka bean, roasted nuts, amber, and warm spices. (Some examples of these include Commodity’s Tonka Eau de Parfum and Parfums de Marly Oajan.) “They still have that cozy feeling people love, but they feel more sophisticated and easier to wear every day.”

DashDividers_1_500x100

The fragrance notes to look out for

When it comes to the fragrance notes catching West’s attention, she’s gravitating toward unexpected combinations that feel modern but effortless. “One of my favorite parts of my job is discovering new brands and seeing how they’re approaching fragrance differently,” she says. Lately, that means soft woods and musks paired with prim florals or airy tea notes — combinations she describes as easy to wear — and scents that “somehow become even better throughout the day.”

One fragrance at the top of her list is Phlur Vanilla Skin, a Nordstrom-exclusive duo (which is sadly sold out) that includes an Eau de Parfum and Hair & Body Fragrance Mist. “It takes vanilla in a much more elevated direction,” says West, pointing to its blend of creamy vanilla, pink pepper, sugar, cashmere, and sandalwood. The result is a warm, layered gourmand that has an addictive, skin-like quality. “It’s the kind of gourmand that isn’t overly sweet, making it incredibly wearable from day to night,” she says.

DashDividers_1_500x100

The unexpected pick to try this season

For a less obvious autumn pick, West recommends Le Labo An0ther 13, a fragrance that proves fall scents don’t necessarily need to be heavy, smoky, or spicy.

“This fall, I’ve been reaching for Le Labo An0ther 13,” she says. The fragrance combines creamy musk, soft woods, and a touch of spice, while woody ambrox gives it the clean, skin-like quality West finds particularly addictive. Jasmine and moss add dimension without weighing it down.

“It’s one of those fragrances that feels effortless and becomes part of you rather than announcing itself,” she says. “Whether I’m heading into meetings during the day or out to dinner in the evening, it always feels appropriate, and that’s exactly what I want from a signature fall scent.”

DashDividers_1_500x100

Fall scent layering made easy

Fall is also an ideal time to experiment with fragrance layering, and West’s first piece of advice is refreshingly simple: Start with moisturized skin. “It really helps your fragrance last longer,” she says.

From there, she encourages playing around with contrasting fragrance families. “I love pairing a clean musk with a richer vanilla or adding a woody fragrance underneath something brighter to give it a little more depth,” she says. And when it comes to layering, have fun with it: “There really aren’t any rules, and I think that’s why people enjoy it so much.”

title: This Gentle Deodorant Is The Only One I Trust In Summer – & Beyond
text:
This Gentle Deodorant Is The Only One I Trust In Summer – & Beyond

I review products for a living year-round, but if there’s one category that is particularly made for stress-testing, it’s deodorant — specifically in the summer months. Dallas is an especially demanding place to live and manage not to be sweaty and stinky. (The day I’m writing this is a balmy 102°F.) But as someone who has largely broken up with aluminum-based deodorants, I have to admit that it’s been a difficult, and at times smelly, endeavor to stay cool and comfortable. What I thought was an impossible task, however, has been disproven by Oak Essentials’ Microbiome Balancing Deodorant.

The brand, founded by Jenni Kayne of luxury-sweater fame, has become one of my new favorites, and I can’t help but feel like it’s somewhat slept on. Its body products in particular are among the most luxurious and nourishing I’ve tried, with a focus on botanical ingredients like blue tansy, rose oil, olive extract, and sea algae, to name a few. (Oak Essentials even launched a hand-care collection with Jenni Kayne, which is easily my new status hand soap.) But back to the deodorant stick: Keep reading for why it beats every other non-aluminum deodorant in my collection. 

What is Oak Essentials’ Microbiome Balancing Deodorant, and what are the benefits?

In typical antiperspirants, aluminum is the active ingredient that essentially plugs sweat glands to reduce perspiration and wetness. (And while the ingredient isn’t inherently bad, sensitive skin types may find it irritating, particularly after shaving. Then there’s the telltale white residue and yellow marks it can leave on clothing.) Deodorants, by contrast, target odor but won’t necessarily keep you dry or sweat-free. (That distinction alone comes down to personal preference.) As the name suggests, Oak Essentials’ Microbiome Balancing Deodorant aims to not only target B.O. but also to deliver skincare benefits to the underarm skin — which, frankly, goes through a lot. Between regular shaving, sweating, and friction, the skin under your arms deserves — but rarely gets — some T.L.C.

Here’s where a product like Oak Essentials’ deodorant comes in. Since it’s something you may apply several times a day, it’s also an opportunity to give your underarms a little extra skincare love. The stick is formulated with noni fruit stem cells, which the brand says help balance the underarm microbiome (aka the natural community of bacteria on your skin) and keep odor-causing bacteria at bay. In lieu of aluminum salts, magnesium hydroxide helps absorb moisture, while blue tansy — a botanical ingredient often used in acne products to help soothe irritation and visible redness — helps neutralize odor, calm sensitive skin, and also gives the product its a natural periwinkle hue. (Don’t worry, it glides on clear.)

What makes Oak Essentials’ Microbiome Balancing Deodorant special?

I’m not exaggerating when I say this is the only aluminum-free deodorant I’ve been able to wear in the summer without worrying about B.O. I work out often and sweat a lot, and this kept up with all of it. Even on those aggressively hot Dallas days, I never found myself doing the subtle underarm sniff test halfway through the day, which, for an aluminum-free deodorant, is saying something. (I will say, this won’t stop you from sweating, so if that’s a dealbreaker, know that going in.)

My lone gripe with this deodorant is that the blue tansy-and-chamomile fragrance is barely noticeable, which was probably intentional so as not to clash with other fragrances. For that reason, I’ll occasionally wear a separate body mist (don’t worry, a gym-friendly one) for a little extra olfactory insurance if I know I’m headed to a packed yoga studio.

As for the skincare benefits, I can’t say I’ve noticed a dramatic difference; that being said, I don’t shave regularly because I’ve had my underarms lasered, so my skin is already starting from a pretty soothed, happy place. That said, it does feel really nice and gentle on the skin — almost like a serum-stick texture — which did hydrate and calm any heat-related redness.

What to know about Oak Essentials’ Microbiome Balancing Deodorant:

• Contains magnesium hydroxide and blue tansy to neutralize odor-causing bacteria.
• Suitable for sensitive skin.
• Soothes irritation and balances the underarm microbiome.

Where can you get Oak Essentials’ Microbiome Balancing Deodorant, and is it worth it?

You can purchase Oak Essentials’ Microbiome Balancing Deodorant for $26 on Oak Essentials’ website, Ulta Beauty, and Nordstrom. And while yes, that’s much pricier than what you would find on drugstore shelves, I will say this stick has lasted me a surprisingly long time — I’m still on my first one and have been using it all summer — and for me, it performs better than drugstore aluminum-free alternatives. And as someone who loves smelling good, the peace of mind I get with this stuff is truly priceless.

title: Olivia Rodrigo’s Serena Joy Is A Powerful Meditation On Solidarity And Resistance
text:
Olivia Rodrigo’s Serena Joy Is A Powerful Meditation On Solidarity And Resistance

Nearly three years after Guts made its way into the world, everyone’s favorite plaid-laden pop icon Olivia Rodrigo returned this June with her third studio album, you seem pretty sad for a girl so in love. A devastatingly raw depiction of the lifecycle of romantic love, the album traces the sweet beginnings of new romance and the head-dizzying hope of finding yourself in someone else. As the record progresses, the threads of the relationship begin to unravel. It’s undoubtedly one of Rodrigo’s most vulnerable bodies of work, earning widespread praise from critics and fans alike and debuting at number one in over 20 countries. In the eight weeks since its release, stupid song and the cure have boomed around my little Hyundai hatchback more times than I’d like to admit, which is why it was such a delightful surprise this week to wake up to the news of the pop star dropping a new standalone track, serena joy.

If that name doesn’t immediately ring a bell and you haven’t yet dived into the dystopian pages of Margaret Atwood’s acclaimed The Handmaid’s Tale, allow me to connect the dots. The novel is set in the dystopian theocracy of Gilead — a society in which women exist almost entirely for their reproductive value, with any sense of autonomy effectively stripped away. Gilead is a world constructed by and for men, where fanatic religious extremism and brutish violence prosper.

Serena Joy, a conservative woman of high social status, is in many ways a purveyor of this system. But what makes her character so complex and compelling is her inevitable fall from grace: the very cage she so diligently helped build becomes her own prison. Rodrigo’s song charts this contradiction, exposing the fate of those who uphold the very structures that entrap them. And while the character may exist in an abstract, fictional universe, the political parallels to modern-day reproductive laws, the rise of the manosphere and the resurgence of right-wing hostility — just look at the current administration — are undeniable.

Though Rodrigo never explicitly references Serena in the song, her essence is unmistakable in the lyrics. The track opens with a powerful statement, delivered in almost spoken-word: “Yeah, it’s all for the cause / For the good of us all / And if you close your eyes / Then it can’t be your fault.” When we talk about systems of oppression, we often focus our energy on those sitting cushy on their throne, unaffected by the weight of their own authority. But rarely do we look outwards to those seemingly on our own side — one foot in our camp, the other carefully balancing the very structures they feel compelled to uphold. There’s a complex, unspoken hostility in being betrayed by those you thought would stand with you. As the track progresses, so too does the urgency of solidarity. “If they do it to them / Thеy’ll do it to you.” It’s almost a call to arms for collective vigilance. Infighting isn’t new; it’s existed since the earliest days of protest.

Yet it still simmers beneath the surface, in terse alliances and uneasy truces, as we fight the more urgent battles against oppression. It’s a tension that begs to be ignored, with many fearing the consequences of breaking the collective silence, which is why it’s so powerful — and profoundly important — that Rodrigo tackles this squarely in her new track. As a young woman with an immense audience, she doesn’t shy away from such a fraught topic, instead giving voice to conversations that are too often silenced. While the release came as a surprise to many (myself included), it certainly isn’t the singer’s first foray into taking aim at systems of oppression and using her voice for advocacy. In 2022 at Glastonbury Festival, she was joined by iconic British artist Lily Allen for a duet of Allen’s anthemic “F*ck You” in protest of the Roe v. Wade ruling in the U.S. Rodrigo has continually shown herself to be a living, breathing, fishnet-wearing example of the power of advocacy.

More recently, Rodrigo called out critics who deemed her babydoll dresses too provocative, exposing the misdirected moral panic with a deft hand: “It’s just this rhetoric that we’re fed as girls since we’re so little, which is like, ‘Don’t wear that because then a man is going to sexualize your body and it’s your fault.’ Like, it’s so weird”. Her activism pokes holes in the patriarchal structures that seek to suffocate women’s autonomy, and serena joy is the next rung on that ladder. The timing of the release is no coincidence, either. Rodrigo’s inaugural Daisy Chain Fields music festival takes place on Saturday, August 29, boasting an all-women lineup, with all net profits going to organizations supporting women and girls.

It’s her rejection of the binary that I find most refreshing. She’s a 23-year-old woman, and she’s not pretending otherwise. She’s navigating heartbreak, self-discovery, political activism and the complexities of growing up in the public eye, all with more gumption than I ever had at that age. Bravo, Olivia. Bravo.

title: The Not Suitable For Work Cancellation Is A Warning Sign For The Future Of TV
text:
The Not Suitable For Work Cancellation Is A Warning Sign For The Future Of TV

The cancellation of Not Suitable For Work after one season has hit fans like a truck. While we’ve all had a favorite TV show ripped away from us far too soon (I’m looking at you My Lady Jane), this cancellation feels different. It’s a warning flare for the kind of messy, horny, occasionally mortifying twenty-something TV that has made streaming feel genuinely fun again.

Hulu opted not to renew Mindy Kaling’s comedy for a second season just two months after its first season ended. The series followed five young professionals in New York navigating jobs, friendships, romance and rent. The first season ended with multiple cliffhangers, a Giggly Squad cameo and a bubbling love triangle that will now haunt me for years to come.

The show was not universally adored by critics. Not Suitable For Work holds a 54% critics’ score on Rotten Tomatoes, although its audience score sits at 82%. It did have its issues — some accused the show of being out of touch and romanticizing corporate America. It reportedly averaged about 800,000 viewers across its first five episodes after 11 days, a figure described by Variety as among Hulu’s lowest-rated programs since 2005. Despite various qualms, there was absolutely an audience warming to it, even if the show had not yet become a full-scale streaming event.

And that’s the problem. Sometimes a show needs time to settle into its characters, learn which dynamics work and let viewers find it without relying on beloved IP. The last few years have offered a genuinely enjoyable wave of twenty-something shows. Adults, Overcompensating and Sterling Point are different beasts, but they share a willingness to let young people be complicated, broke, horny, overly online and, occasionally, deeply annoying. Which is to say: recognizable.

They also feel like they were made by people who understand that Gen Z does not speak in TikTok slop or run exclusively on oat milk-iced matchas (we drink coffee too). The characters make jokes about sex, money, work and their own terrible choices. They are politically aware without sounding like a producer is having an aneurysm off screen about brand safety. At a time when there is endless chatter about Gen Z becoming more conservative, it has been refreshing to see shows that are not afraid to be a bit filthy, emotionally direct and interested in the awkwardness of growing up. Not Suitable For Work was far from perfect, but its premise was clear: your twenties can be chaotic, humiliating and very funny. You can be ambitious and still have no clue what you are doing. You can have a career plan and then immediately set it on fire because someone tall texted you.

When I spoke to Kaling before the show premiered, she explained that she had put parts of herself into each of the five leads. “The joy of making a TV show is that I get to infuse different parts of my personality, the good and the bad, into all of the characters,” she said at the time. She described relating to Davis’s “longing and this neediness to be loved at that age”, particularly the desire for a first serious relationship, “so you can prove to people that there’s nothing wrong with you”. It’s a very specific early-twenties feeling: wanting to appear completely fine while privately treating every minor romantic interaction like a judgement on your entire worth.

Kaling also spoke about writing women’s anger, particularly the pressure on Asian women to suppress it. “I love writing about the rage that women feel that they cannot express,” she said. That emotional messiness was part of what made NSFW work. Abby (Avantika Vandanapu) could be polished and furious, while AJ (Ella Hunt) could be ambitious and out of her depth, and everyone could make the incredibly wrong call for reasons that made perfect sense in the moment. It was not always subtle, but neither are your twenties.

Historically, television has given comedies room to be themselves. Parks and Recreation had a first season that was criticised for feeling too much like The Office before it reworked Leslie Knope (Amy Poehler), expanded its ensemble and became a beloved workplace comedy and my fave gardening show. I personally had to try out Schitt’s Creek three times to make it through (and understand) season one in order to get the rest of the show, which is a masterpiece.

The idea that a comedy might need a few episodes to figure itself out was not once treated as a moral failing. This is not an argument that every underperforming show should be granted indefinite life support. Sometimes a series does not find its footing, and that is television. We have been saved from enduring more of some truly terrible shows. But original comedies without book-fandom hype, a recognisable intellectual property label or a cast of household names are now being asked to arrive fully formed, instantly beloved, perfectly marketable and capable of triggering discourse before the opening credits have ended.

Meanwhile, adaptations and reboots arrive with their fandoms pre-loaded. They have readers or die-hard fans who already know the characters, built-in social-media discussion and a marketing hook that can be explained in four words: “It’s based on the book”. Original storytelling has to work much harder just to get people to press play. It’s not like Hulu is even against a multi-season moment. The streamer currently has 22 seasons and 466 episodes of Grey’s Anatomy available to watch, meaning Meredith Grey (Ellen Pompeo) has had approximately 253,863 opportunities to endure an absurdly stressful day at work.

So, yes, there is room for a show to last. The question is which ones get that chance. Hulu / Disney+ already had Adults on its roster, but surely a platform can support more than one series about people in their twenties. Prime Video has made a noticeable habit of commissioning YA fare. Hulu and Disney+ could have owned the slightly older, sharper and more adult version of that space: stories about the post-uni years, the early career grind and the humiliating gap between how put-together you look online and how little you understand your superannuation.

Instead, Not Suitable For Work has been cancelled after one season, with its characters left suspended in romantic and professional chaos. Warner Bros. Television is reportedly shopping the series elsewhere, so there may still be hope for a second life.

But the cancellation should still worry anyone invested in original young-adult television. If streamers keep giving new shows barely enough time to establish an audience, viewers may eventually stop investing in them altogether. Why fall in love with a messy group of fictional twenty-somethings when there is every chance they will be gone before they have even made it through their first proper workplace meltdown?

From PEDESTRIAN.TV

title: The Last Eclipse Of Summer Is Here — & It’ll Mark A Symbolic Shift For You
text:
The Last Eclipse Of Summer Is Here — & It’ll Mark A Symbolic Shift For You

The last eclipse of summer has arrived! Cosmic beings, the partial Lunar Eclipse in Pisces occurs on August 28th at 12:18 a.m. ET. Take note because we’re finalizing the cycle that began back in September, 2024. Making peace with ourselves, particularly our hearts, will give us the stamina to forge a new path. Of course, the cosmos are throwing curveballs our way to ensure we are progressing with the natural rhythm of the world.

As you know, a partial eclipse (and all eclipses) brings the unforeseen to light, since the Earth moves between the sun and the Full Moon, casting an imperfect shadow that blocks sunlight. Only part of the moon moves into the Earth’s shadow, known as “the umbra.” Eclipses are catalysts for transformation — on a global and personal level. They speak to the general state of the collective and push us to change. Societal and cultural shifts happen, as one era ends and another begins with the thrill of whimsy and wonder.

Simply put, a lunar eclipse (regardless of whether it’s partial or not) is an extremely potent Full Moon that is activated by the karmic Nodes of Destiny. This is one of the last eclipses on the Pisces and Virgo axis, and it is going to mark a symbolic shift in our consciousness. Emotions will intensify, and situations will culminate, resulting in us letting go of old feelings and resentments as we move into a heightened state of glory. However, the journey to enlightenment is not going to come easy. On the road to discovering our new sense of being, there will be revelations that might be frustrating.

The lesson is to listen to what is being shown to us at this juncture. Eclipses are fateful celestial events that motivate us to make major decisions when we are ready. If we don’t incite necessary change at some point, then the stars will do it for us in the most provocative way; therefore, the best advice is to accept the epiphany with open arms and a grain of salt, knowing that it’s not now or never, and that we have an exponential amount of time to discuss and work on what is divulged. The world keeps on spinning and we must keep up with its pace. Also, nothing is ever really over, it evolves into something else, which could be greater.

The day before the eclipse, Mercury cazimi in Virgo gives us perspective on matters that need clarity. The sun’s affiliation with Mercury brightens our minds by illuminating situations that have been unresolved or in need of more explanation. The quest for information is the energy we are bringing into the eclipse. With Mercury in Virgo and Uranus in Gemini creating a T-Square (a tense astrological aspect that forms a T shape in the sky), the news coming to us will be explosive and exciting. It’ll lead us to a flash of transparency and clarity. 

Further, the centaur Chiron (”the wounded healer”), which is retrograde in Taurus, fortifies our ability to strengthen our essence and resolve by resolving issues that have been lingering for a while. The asteroid Ceres in Cancer (who represents unconditional love) offers us tenderness and self-love as we navigate the erratic waters of the eclipse. Chiron and Ceres are our saving grace, allowing us not to falter, but to gain courage to grow and transcend. The tides are changing in our favor; have patience and be kind (to ourselves and others). A constructive endeavor for the eclipse would be to honor our spirit with gratitude for our own amazingness.

The “a-ha” moment may come through different realms. Our dreams have significance in our daily actions, which is why we should journal these visions when we are contemplating them in the morning. The astral plane is popping, bringing past connections and present events into our minds from our subconscious. We hold the key to understanding our thoughts and desires, as well as what we want in the future. Tuning into our intuition is the way to move forward and release our emotions. The universe is waking us up from our slumber, showing us how to heal and navigate the next phase of life. Ready or not, it’s happening!
